# Preface {.unnumbered}

::: epigraph
> It seems that perfection is attained, not when there is nothing more to add,
> but when there is nothing more to take away.
>
> ---Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, *Wind, Sand and Stars* (1939, trans. Lewis Galantière)
:::

Many reports end up with tables in them. Not glamorous ones: a few rows, a few
columns, a title, a footnote that says *"p-values are two-sided"*. Getting such
humble tables to look right often takes more effort than the analysis they
summarize.

The **lt** package is my attempt to make tables boring again, in the good sense.
You hand it a data frame, pipe it through a handful of small verbs, and get
back a table that already looks like it belongs in a publication:

```{r}
d = data.frame(
  Group = c("Treatment", "Treatment", "Control", "Control"),
  Endpoint = c("Primary", "Secondary", "Primary", "Secondary"),
  Estimate = c(0.6123, 0.7891, 0.4567, 0.5432),
  CI_Lower = c(0.4012, 0.5678, 0.2345, 0.3210),
  CI_Upper = c(0.8234, 1.0104, 0.6789, 0.7654),
  P_Value = c(0.0012, NA, 0.1234, NA)
)
lt(d) |>
  lt_group(~ Group) |>
  lt_header("Study Results", "Primary and secondary endpoints") |>
  lt_spanner(`95% CI` ~ CI_Lower + CI_Upper) |>
  lt_format(~ Estimate + CI_Lower + CI_Upper, decimals = 3) |>
  lt_sub(~ P_Value, missing = "n/a") |>
  lt_footnote("Two-sided p-value from log-rank test.", "column", ~ P_Value)
```

That is the whole idea. The rest of this book is about the details, and there
are more of them than the pitch suggests: **lt** can also draw forest plots
and sparklines inside cells, turn a table into an interactive explorer with
filters and plain-language search, serve a million rows from R without
breaking a sweat, and become an editable input in a Shiny app.

## Why another table package?

The origin story is a small moment of shock. A project required
[**gt**](https://gt.rstudio.com), so I ran `install.packages("gt")` in a fresh R
session on Linux, and watched R install one package after another, as if it were
going to install half of CRAN. Some had to be compiled, and a few took ages
(**V8** in particular). I wondered whether I had mistyped something, because surely a
table package could not need *this* much. That was when I learned how deep
**gt**'s recursive dependency tree goes.

**gt** has a beautiful grammar of tables, and **lt** owes it the inspiration.
[**DT**](https://github.com/rstudio/DT) makes tables interactive, but ships a
whole JavaScript library with it. I wanted the vocabulary of the former and the
interactivity of the latter in something I could install in a heartbeat and read
in an afternoon. So I asked a question I keep asking: how small can this be if I
only care about HTML? The answer turned out to be *quite* small, with a few
deliberate trade-offs:

-   **HTML first.** In HTML I trust: it reflows, it styles with a line of CSS,
    and it opens on any phone. Every other format starts from HTML. PDF, PNG,
    and RTF can all be generated from a browser, which almost every machine
    already has (see @chp:export). Once you commit to HTML, an enormous amount
    of complexity simply evaporates.

-   **One dependency.** **lt** imports **xfun**, and that is all. No sass, no V8,
    no htmltools.

-   **A tiny runtime.** R does not render the `<table>`. It ships your data and
    a short list of instructions as JSON, and a small, plain JavaScript file
    (about 10 KB minified, no framework, no build step) builds the table in the
    browser. A page full of tables loads that file once.

-   **Pay for what you use.** Inline plots and interactivity live in separate
    extensions that a page loads only when some table asks for them. A plain
    table never pays for sorting it doesn't have.

I don't want to match **gt** or **DT** feature for feature. I want to cover the
table structure most reports actually need, and to show that if you are willing
to trust HTML, you can go a remarkably long way with remarkably little.

## How it works

```{pele}
#| how-it-works, echo = FALSE,
#| fig.cap = 'From a data frame to a table: R describes, the browser draws.'

flowchart LR
  A[data frame] -->|"lt() |> lt_*()"| B[("data + instructions<br>(JSON)")]
  B -->|"lt.js in<br>browser"| C[table]
```

Each `lt_*()` function records an instruction (*format this column*, *group
those rows*, *add a footnote here*) on the table object without touching the
data. When the table is printed, the data and instructions travel to the page as
a compact JSON spec, and the runtime applies them. Because the spec is plain
JSON, nice things follow:

-   **Any language can drive it.** All the table logic lives in the JavaScript
    runtime, once, and knows nothing about R. The R package is a thin front end
    that writes JSON; a Python or Julia package could be another, with no second
    implementation of the table engine, just a different keyboard for the same
    piano. You can also build a table straight from JavaScript (@chp:js).

-   **The truth is always one hover away.** The browser holds the original data,
    so formatting never throws values away. Hover over a cell to see its raw
    value, or press <kbd>Alt</kbd> and click the table to reveal all of them. We
    no longer have to argue about the right number of decimal places: readers
    can always look underneath, which a static PDF or image can never offer.

-   **Other tools can embed an lt table**, by shipping the spec and calling
    `LT.render()` (@chp:export).

## Installation

Install the released version from CRAN, or the development version from
r-universe:

```r
# CRAN version
install.packages("lt")

# development version
install.packages("lt", repos = "https://yihui.r-universe.dev")
```

You can also play with the package in your browser, with nothing installed, at
<https://pkg.yihui.org/lt/playground/>.

## How to read this book

The chapters follow the life of a table. We start with a first table
(@chp:start), then teach it to format numbers (@chp:format), shape its rows and
columns (@chp:structure), explain itself (@chp:notes), draw (@chp:plots), and
dress up (@chp:style). After that comes the fun part: making it interactive
(@chp:interactive), putting it in Shiny apps (@chp:shiny), and getting it out of
R (@chp:export). Two chapters stand apart: one for those who want to use the
JavaScript runtime directly (@chp:js), and one for those arriving from **gt**
(@chp:gt).

Almost every code block here is a small, self-contained example that lives in
the [`examples/`](https://github.com/yihui/lt/tree/main/examples) folder of the
package, one feature per file. The link under a block ("Open as a page") opens
it on its own, so you can read the source, view the table at full width, or copy
the file as a starting point. If you would rather learn by poking, the
[playground](https://pkg.yihui.org/lt/playground/) is the place.

Throughout, we use the native pipe `|>`.
